description: Width tiers for HASS Foundation — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor. K-strand descriptors use phenomena_contexts; S-strand descriptors use task_contexts.
subject: HASS

width_notes.minimum_width: For K-strand (Knowledge) descriptors: the narrowest set of phenomena or contexts that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term — typically one family structure, one place, or one celebration. For S-strand (Skills/Inquiry) descriptors: the narrowest task context in which the skill is applied — one source type, one familiar topic, one presentation mode.
width_notes.typical_width: For K-strand descriptors: engagement across the range of examples indicated by elaborations — multiple family types, place features, or celebration types as the descriptor scope requires. For S-strand descriptors: the skill applied across two or more task types or contexts representative of the elaboration range.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, cultural contexts, or task contexts — not harder versions of the same. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider where present in ACARA source material.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data to ground typical_width and identify wider directions. Not treated as a required checklist — elaborations at similar specificity are merged. First Nations elaborations consistently placed in wider.

AC9HSFK01.minimum_width: Identify members of their own immediate family, where they were born, and how family members are related to each other.
AC9HSFK01.typical_width: Describe a range of family members including extended family, where different members were born and raised, and how they are connected; acknowledge that family structures vary across students.
wider: Explore varieties of kinship structure from different cultural backgrounds — for example, how First Nations Australian families use terms like 'cousin-brother' and 'mother-auntie' to describe extended kin relationships
Create concept maps or drawings that show family connections across two or more generations, including places of birth and childhood
elaborations: discussing the members of a family (for example, mother, father, caregiver, sister, brother, grandparent, auntie, uncle, cousin) and acknowledging other varieties of kinship structure that may be represented in the cultural background of students (for example, cousin-brother and mother-auntie in First Nations Australian families)
creating drawings of family members accompanied by information collected from questions and observations to share details of that person's life, including the places they were born and raised
creating concept maps of their family with pictures or photographs to show connections to those people who make up their family

AC9HSFK02.minimum_width: Identify one or two celebrations or commemorations shared with family and explain why they are important.
AC9HSFK02.typical_width: Describe a range of celebrations and commemorations shared with family and community — including birthdays, religious festivals, cultural events, and national commemorations such as NAIDOC Week and Anzac Day — and explain why they matter.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians pass on traditions through art, music, storytelling, and family gatherings as part of cultural celebrations
Compare celebrations from two or more different cultural or religious backgrounds represented in the class community
elaborations: responding to a provided calendar of events that students, their family and friends celebrate or commemorate; for example, birthdays; religious festivals such as Easter, Ramadan, Buddha's Birthday, Feast of Passover and Coming of the Light; family reunions; cultural festivals; and community commemorations such as NAIDOC Week and Anzac Day, and discussing why they are important

discussing ways of celebrating these significant occasions; for example, special meals, family gatherings, visiting special places, and the role of art, music, telling stories and handing on traditions from generation to generation for First Nations Australians

AC9HSFK03.minimum_width: Identify one familiar place they belong to and explain why it is special to them.
AC9HSFK03.typical_width: Describe the features of several familiar places they belong to or are aware of; explain why some places are special; discuss different ways people can care for places.
wider: Investigate the meaning of Country/Place for First Nations Australians and identify how their local area connects to a specific Country/Place, including reasons people maintain cultural connections to Country/Place
Explore imaginary or distant places from stories, television or family accounts, comparing their features with familiar local places
elaborations: identifying the places, communities, Country/Place they live in and belong to and why that place may be special to them; for example, a neighbourhood, suburb, town or rural locality, community

exploring the features of their own place, and places they are familiar with or aware of; for example, places they have visited, places family members have come from, imaginary places in stories, or places featured on television and websites, in books or ebooks

identifying reasons why people live in or visit places, such as the provision of basic needs (water, food, shelter), to enhance lives (holiday places, places for recreation, for religious observance) and to maintain cultural connections to Country/Place

discussing different ways they could or do contribute to caring for special places, including those that are unique; for example, planting trees for a local endangered species, cleaning up litter at a local park or beach, or planting flora in a local wetland

AC9HSFK04.minimum_width: Identify the Country/Place on which the school is located and explain what 'Country/Place' means to First Nations Australians.
AC9HSFK04.typical_width: Identify and use the name of the local First Nations Australians' language group(s); describe local places of significance to First Nations Australians; explain why Country/Place is important.
wider: Listen and respond to Traditional Owner community members talking about Country/Place and places of cultural and historical significance in the local area
Compare how First Nations Australians' connections to Country/Place differ from common ways non-Indigenous Australians talk about 'home' or 'neighbourhood'
elaborations: identifying how and why the words "Country/Place" are used by First Nations Australians for the places they belong to
identifying and using the name of the local First Nations Australians' language group or groups

listening and responding to invited members of the Traditional Owner group talking about Country/Place, and places of cultural and historical significance to the First Nations Australian community in the local neighbourhood, suburb, town or rural area
identifying local places of significance for First Nations Australians in the local area

AC9HSFS01.minimum_width: Pose at least one question about a familiar object, person, place or event after a guided observation or source exploration.
AC9HSFS01.typical_width: Pose questions about family, places and events across several source types (photographs, interviews, excursions, observation); generate questions that go beyond 'what' to include 'why' and 'how'.
wider: Pose questions about what makes places special to different people — including family members, community members, and First Nations Australians — after engaging with diverse sources
Generate questions independently before, during and after exploring a source (not only when prompted), demonstrating emerging inquiry habit
elaborations: posing questions about family and places, such as "How old was I?", "Where was I?" and "What was I doing?", having explored sources relating to their own life; for example, family interviews, photographs, stories, film, classmates' paintings, excursions to places
posing questions about the features of places and how they can look after them, after being encouraged to observe them using various senses
posing questions about what makes events and places special; for example "What special events do my family celebrate?", "What makes my favourite places special?"

AC9HSFS02.minimum_width: Sort provided sources (pictures or photographs) into a simple category or sequence; identify features on a provided pictorial map.
AC9HSFS02.typical_width: Sort and record information from sources including historical pictures and photographs; create a pictorial timeline of events; locate and link features on a pictorial map or aerial photograph.
wider: Create an annotated pictorial display combining a timeline and a map to show both the when and the where of a family event or significant place
Collect and sort information independently from more than one source type (for example, family interview plus photographs) and organise it into a coherent display
elaborations: sorting and displaying sources (for example, historical sources such as pictures, photographs and family mementoes) to organise a display about a family member or significant family event and creating pictorial timelines, such as adding photos or drawings of significant events as they happen, to create a timeline of events over the year

identifying features on a provided pictorial map or oblique aerial photograph of a familiar place and linking the representation of specific features to pictures they have drawn of those features; for example, using a pictorial map of a visited site such as a public garden or an oblique aerial photograph of their school to find familiar features, and then linking drawings of those features with lines to the features in the map or aerial photograph

AC9HSFS03.minimum_width: Share one perspective on a special place or significant event drawn from a provided source.
AC9HSFS03.typical_width: Share perspectives on stories about significant events from the past and on special places in their local area; explain why places or events are personally meaningful.
wider: Compare their own perspective on a special place with that of a family member or community member, identifying similarities and differences in what makes a place meaningful
Explore how First Nations Australians' connections to Country/Place represent a different kind of perspective on what makes a place special, using stories or invited speakers as source material
elaborations: sharing aspects of events special to past generations of their family from provided stories and discussing why those events and places are special
identifying a place in their local area that they like, and talking about why they like it and how they could care for it

AC9HSFS04.minimum_width: Draw a simple conclusion in response to one guided question — for example, identify who the main people in their family are and how they are related.
AC9HSFS04.typical_width: Draw conclusions in response to questions across topic areas — family, celebrations, places — using information gathered from sources and observations.
wider: Draw conclusions that connect across topics — for example, explaining how caring for a special place connects to why it matters to a community or family
Propose specific actions they will take to care for a place (classroom, bedroom, playground) and explain the reasoning behind the proposal
elaborations: identifying the main people in their family and explaining how they are related
identifying the most important celebrations and commemorations in their lives and those of their family
exploring the location and features of places they belong to and what makes those places special
suggesting ways that they are going to care for their classroom, bedroom or playground

AC9HSFS05.minimum_width: Share one narrative or observation about a special place or family event using pictures, drawings or spoken words; use at least one time or location term correctly.
AC9HSFS05.typical_width: Create a display or narrative about a special place or family event using photographs, artefacts and/or drawings; use subject-specific terms for time (then, now, yesterday) and location (near, far, above, below) appropriately.
wider: Present narratives using more than one mode — for example, combining spoken narrative with drawings and a simple map or timeline
Use both time terms and location terms in the same presentation to situate an event or place in when and where
elaborations: creating a display about a special place or family event using photographs, artefacts and/or drawings
using terms about time when talking about their experiences; for example, "then", "now", "yesterday", "today", "tomorrow"
using appropriate terms to describe the direction and location of a place such as "near and far", "above and below", "beside and opposite"
